content: The synthetic conjugated estrogens, B, are absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract after being released from the drug formulation. ENJUVIA tablets release these synthetic conjugated estrogens slowly over several hours. A study involving 21 healthy postmenopausal women under fasting conditions was conducted using 0.625 mg tablets. The effect of food on the bioavailability of synthetic conjugated estrogens, B, following ENJUVIA administration has not been studied. However, food did not significantly affect the pharmacokinetics of a similar formulation of synthetic conjugated estrogens, B. The distribution of exogenous estrogens is comparable to that of endogenous estrogens. Estrogens are widely distributed throughout the body, with higher concentrations typically found in sex hormone target organs. In the bloodstream, estrogens are primarily bound to sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) and albumin. Exogenous estrogens are metabolized in the same manner as endogenous estrogens. Circulating estrogens exist in a dynamic equilibrium of metabolic interconversions, which predominantly occur in the liver. Estradiol is reversibly converted to estrone, and both can be further converted to estriol, the major urinary metabolite. Estrogens also undergo enterohepatic recirculation, involving sulfate and glucuronide conjugation in the liver, biliary secretion of these conjugates into the intestine, hydrolysis in the intestine, and subsequent reabsorption. In postmenopausal women, a significant portion of circulating estrogens exists as sulfate conjugates, particularly estrone sulfate, which serves as a circulating reservoir for the formation of more active estrogens. Estradiol, estrone, and estriol are excreted in the urine along with their glucuronide and sulfate conjugates. The mean (± SD) apparent terminal elimination half-life (t½) of conjugated estrone is 14 (± 6) hours, and for conjugated equilin, it is 11 (± 6) hours. No pharmacokinetic studies have been conducted in special populations, including patients with renal or hepatic impairment. There is limited pharmacokinetic information available regarding synthetic conjugated estrogens, B, in the drug label. Long-term continuous administration of natural and synthetic estrogens in certain animal species has been associated with an increased frequency of carcinomas in the breast, uterus, cervix, vagina, testis, and liver. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging, multi-center clinical study was conducted to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of ENJUVIA tablets for the treatment of vasomotor symptoms. The study included 281 naturally or surgically postmenopausal women aged 26 to 65 years who experienced at least seven moderate to severe hot flushes per day or 50 per week at randomization. Four percent of the participants were Black (n = 49). Participants received either 0.3 mg, 0.625 mg, 1.25 mg, or placebo once daily for 12 weeks. The 0.625 mg dose was shown to be statistically superior to placebo at weeks 4 and 12 in reducing both the frequency and severity of moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms.
